meta.description: Not Confucius. Ogden Nash wrote the billboard couplet in Song of the Open Road, The New Yorker, October 15, 1932 - a parody of Joyce Kilmer's Trees.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Think that I Shall Never See a Billboard Lovely as a Tree'?
meta.ogDescription: Ogden Nash, not Confucius. The billboard-and-tree couplet ran in The New Yorker on October 15, 1932, parodying Joyce Kilmer's poem Trees.

answer.label: Not Confucius — actually Ogden Nash
answer.sourceLine: The couplet opens “Song of the Open Road,” a four-line squib by Ogden Nash printed in The New Yorker of October 15, 1932 — a parody of Joyce Kilmer’s “Trees.” Quote Investigator traces the Confucius credit to a March 1940 newspaper reader contest in Harlingen, Texas whose “Confucius Say” ascriptions were never meant seriously.

source.heading: The 1932 printing

docMeta.dd: The Face Is Familiar: The Selected Verse of Ogden Nash, 1940 (“Indeed” for “Perhaps”)

source.excerpt:
I think that I shall never see
A billboard lovely as a tree.
trail: October 15, 1932 — The New Yorker prints “Song of the Open Road” over Ogden Nash’s name; Quote Investigator calls this the earliest publication it has found ↗.
November 1932 — the verse is already loose in the newspapers, printed in Spearfish, South Dakota as “Nother Pome” and in Bessemer, Michigan with the accurate credit “Ogden Nash in the New Yorker” ↗.

1940 — Nash reprints it in The Face Is Familiar: The Selected Verse of Ogden Nash with “Indeed” replacing “Perhaps”; weeks earlier a Texas paper had run it as a “Confucius Say” contest entry, both documented in QI’s citation list ↗.

The joke depends on Joyce Kilmer’s “Trees,” first published in Poetry: A Magazine of Verse in August 1913 and collected in Trees and Other Poems in 1914 — Wikipedia’s account of the poem ↗ also records Nash’s billboard parody.
source.excerptNote: Only the opening couplet is reproduced here: the poem is four lines long and still under copyright. In the 1932 magazine text the third line begins “Perhaps”; in Nash’s 1940 selected verse he changed it to “Indeed.” The full 1932 text sits in The New Yorker’s archive ↗.

author.name: Ogden Nash
author.heading: Who Ogden Nash was
author.metaLine: 1902–1971 · American poet of light verse; New Yorker contributor
author.bio: Ogden Nash was born in Rye, New York, in 1902 and died in Baltimore in 1971. He made his name with deliberately lopsided rhymes and stretched-out lines, publishing his first collection, Hard Lines, in 1931 and briefly working on The New Yorker’s editorial staff that same year after Harold Ross responded warmly to his submissions. He wrote more than five hundred pieces of light verse, of which the billboard quatrain is among the most quoted — and the most often stripped of his name.

misattribution.heading: How Confucius got the credit
misattribution.intro: Confucius lived in China around 551–479 BCE and had no opinions on roadside advertising. The credit is a residue of a 1930s American newspaper joke format, not of anything in the Confucian corpus.

items.why: The earliest Confucius version Quote Investigator records is a reader-contest entry in the Valley Morning Star of Harlingen, Texas on March 9, 1940, in a column headed “Confucius Say” where every submission carried that prefix; QI notes the ascription was not intended to be taken seriously ↗.

In November 1932, within weeks of publication, the Queen City Mail of Spearfish, South Dakota reprinted the lines under the comic ascription “Nother Pome” — a pun on “another poem” — while the Bessemer Herald that same month credited “Ogden Nash in the New Yorker” ↗.

The 1932 magazine text begins the third line “Perhaps”; Nash himself replaced it with “Indeed” for his 1940 selected verse, and an Iowa garden column printed “And soon” in 1938 — all three are documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The lines are Ogden Nash’s, printed under his name in The New Yorker on October 15, 1932; Quote Investigator credits the work to Nash ↗, and the magazine’s own archive carries his byline on it ↗.

context.heading: Why a joke about billboards outlived its author’s name
lead: Joyce Kilmer’s “Trees” was, by 1932, the most recited poem in America — which made its opening line the perfect thing to hijack. Nash kept Kilmer’s first line intact, swapped one noun in the second, and turned a hymn to nature into a complaint about roadside advertising. The gag works because the reader supplies the original.

Newspapers picked it up within weeks, and it escaped almost immediately. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows a South Dakota paper running it in November 1932 under the comic byline “Nother Pome,” a Macon garden-club speaker paraphrasing it that December, and an Iowa garden column printing an altered third line in 1938. By the time it reached a Texas “Confucius Say” contest in March 1940, the verse had been circulating unattached to its author for years.
detailsBody: The “Confucius Say” format was a 1930s American joke fad, not a claim about Chinese philosophy: papers invited readers to send in adages prefaced by the phrase, and printed them. Quote Investigator observes that competitions of this kind help explain the artificially amplified ubiquity of Confucius attributions. The entry that ran in the Valley Morning Star of Harlingen, Texas on March 9, 1940 was submitted by a reader, Mrs. Arthur J. Carpenter of Rio Hondo, and used Nash’s original “Perhaps” wording.

Even the “correct” version is unstable, because Nash revised it himself. If you want the text as it first appeared, the third line begins “Perhaps”; if you want the text Nash settled on for his 1940 selected verse, it begins “Indeed.” Both are his.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator credits the billboard verse to Ogden Nash, names The New Yorker of October 15, 1932 (page 18, col. 2) as the earliest publication known to QI, records the 1940 'Indeed' revision in The Face Is Familiar, the 'Nother Pome' and Bessemer Herald reprints of November 1932, the 1938 'And soon' variant from Malvern, Iowa, and the March 9, 1940 'Confucius Say' contest entry in the Valley Morning Star of Harlingen, Texas, noting that ascription was not meant to be taken seriously.
The New Yorker's own archive page for 'Song of the Open Road' is bylined Ogden Nash, is filed under the October 15, 1932 issue, and carries the four-line text whose third line begins 'Perhaps'.

Wikiquote's Ogden Nash page lists the billboard quatrain in the 'Indeed' wording under the title 'Song of the Open Road', notes it parodies Joyce Kilmer's 'Trees', and gives Nash's life dates as 19 August 1902 – 19 May 1971.
Joyce Kilmer's 'Trees' was first published in Poetry: A Magazine of Verse in August 1913 and collected in Trees and Other Poems (1914); the article also quotes Ogden Nash's billboard parody.
Project Gutenberg's text of Joyce Kilmer's Trees and Other Poems (1914) contains the poem 'Trees', opening 'I think that I shall never see / A poem lovely as a tree.'

Ogden Nash was born in Rye, New York on August 19, 1902 and died in Baltimore on May 19, 1971; he wrote more than 500 pieces of light verse, published his first collection Hard Lines in 1931, and spent three months in 1931 on The New Yorker's editorial staff after Harold Ross responded to his submissions.
Quote Investigator's Confucius category page lists the billboard/tree investigation alongside many other sayings popularly credited to Confucius that QI traces to other origins.
Wikipedia gives Confucius's dates as c. 551 – c. 479 BCE.
